extracted.intended_audience: economic historians, empirical economists, and policy researchers studying inequality and New Deal–era programs
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of income and housing inequality (and top-end measures) across U.S. cities and counties between 1929 and 1940, using Gini coefficients, rent-based measures, and taxpayer counts and relating them to New Deal programs and local economic changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income Gini (family incomes, city level)
rubrics_metrics.description: An income gini based on family incomes in 1929 for 33 cities and in 1933 for up to 48 cities that describes inequality throughout the income distribution in cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculated from Mendershausen’s 11 income bins (1929 and 1933) and used to compare levels and changes across cities; family income includes cash income from all sources, including relief payments, but excludes the value of free rent or other in-kind income. Examine changes between 1929 and 1933 and relate to state per capita income drops and city/county relief spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housing Gini (contract rents and implicit rents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gini coefficients based on contract rents for renters and implicit rents for homeowners using rent/value bins reported by Census and mid-1930s surveys to measure housing inequality in cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses standard reported nominal bins (seven rent bins for large cities and five bins for smaller cities) with implicit rents for owner-occupied homes taken as 1/100th of home value; expands coverage to ~950+ cities (1930/1940) and to ~141 cities in mid-1930s; compare housing ginis to income ginis (correlations ~0.8 for levels, ~0.6 for changes) as validation. Note that mixing implicit rents and contract rents treats homeowners like renters and likely understates inequality (does not give extra value for housing wealth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-end inequality: taxpayers per family (county level)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rough measure of top-end inequality calculated as the number of federal taxpayers per family in counties for 1930, 1934, and 1939.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data from Rand McNally, U.S. Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, and Internal Revenue mimeos. This is a crude top-end measure; authors note the surprising negative correlation with income and housing ginis in some comparisons and caution about interpretation. Used to analyze inequality across rural and urban areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition matrices across income bins (mobility analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of transition matrices from Mendershausen’s data showing the percentage of families moving from a 1929 income bin to a 1933 bin to study mobility and distributional changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine nominal-bin transitions (11 bins), report shares falling by one or more bins, and interpret with inflation/deflation adjustments (24.5% deflation between 1929 and 1933). Treat falling by two or more nominal bins as a clearer indicator of real purchasing-power loss but note this underestimates true real-income loss for some starting bins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflation/deflation adjustment for real comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust nominal income and dollar measures to a common year's purchasing power (e.g., convert to 1929 dollars using BLS cost indices) when comparing across 1929–1933 and 1930–1940.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors apply a 24.5% deflation adjustment between 1929 and 1933 for interpretation of transitions and average income changes; all dollar values used in some regressions are adjusted to 1967$ (series E-135) for New Deal program amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression specification and interpretation (OLS in logs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use OLS regressions with variables in natural logs so coefficients can be read as elasticities (e.g., change in ln(gini) regressed on change in ln(state real per capita income) and other covariates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include controls such as per capita relief spending, demographic features, and city/county characteristics; be attentive to sample size limitations (e.g., 23-city sample when per capita relief is available) and interpret coefficients and standard errors (robust, clustered at state level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental variable approach for endogenous relief spending
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument per capita relief spending with political variables to address potential endogeneity between relief and inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruments used include presence of a Democratic governor in 1928, percent Democrat in the state upper house, mean share voting Democrat for President 1896–1928, and the standard deviation of that share. Report instrument strength (first-stage F-statistic was 4.91 — not particularly strong) and interpret IV results cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample design and survey coverage (CWA Financial Survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CWA Financial Survey employed a house-to-house canvas of every tenth block in large cities (every seventh in smaller cities) plus mail-back forms in other blocks; coverage ~15% of city populations with ~1% refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the sampling rules (one-in-ten/one-in-seven block selection with informed local-agency augmentation) and the two-stage collection (enumerator canvass and distributed forms) when assessing representativeness and standard errors for city-level measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bin definitions and concordance for housing/value-to-rent conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Census/agency nominal housing-value bins (seven bins for larger cities; five bins for smaller cities) and convert home values to implicit rents at 1/100th of value; alternative concordances considered for 1930 vs 1940.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note implied discount rates (e.g., 11.54% for thirty-year, 10.3% for twenty-year, 8.4% for 15-year, 3.4% for 10-year) when interpreting 1/100th concordance; for cities >50k more detailed bins available. Be explicit about which binning (5-bin vs 7-bin) is used in each comparison and when extending coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of homeowners vs renters in housing inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit rents for homeowners are used alongside contract rents for renters; this mixes flow-of-housing-service measures with ownership status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that treating owners like renters (without an owner-occupation wealth boost) likely understates true inequality if housing is seen as wealth; consider alternative adjustments if the research question demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-measure validation (correlation between measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess correlations between different inequality measures (income ginis, housing ginis, and taxpayers-per-family) to validate whether they capture similar distributional features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report strong correlations: housing and income ginis ~0.8 for levels and ~0.6 for changes; correlations and divergence (e.g., taxpayers measure behavior) should be used to judge comparability and limits of each measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and county-level control variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Include controls such as county population, percent black, percent foreign-born, percent illiterate, and age-structure shares in regressions explaining inequality measures and changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demographic data sourced from 1930 county-level ICPSR datasets; include these variables to parse mechanisms (e.g., urbanization, population growth) that correlate with changes in ginis or taxpayers per family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period selection and multiple comparison windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare multiple periods (e.g., 1929–1933, 1930–1940, 1934–1930, 1936–1930, 1940–1930) to study dynamics of inequality and program effects across short and longer horizons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose period windows appropriate to the data source (e.g., Mendershausen 1929/1933 income bins, census housing 1930/1940) and be cautious in attributing causal effects when program timing (FERA, CWA) occurs late in a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of small-sample / missing-variable issues
rubrics_metrics.description: When key variables (e.g., per capita relief spending) are unavailable for some units, use reduced samples (e.g., 23-city sample) and compare qualitative results to larger samples where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report differences in sample sizes across specifications, test robustness by estimating models without the missing covariate on the larger sample, and note any changes in statistical significance or coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-share calculation constraints using tax data
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculation of top-1% or top-5% shares from federal tax data may be infeasible in jurisdictions where fewer than 5% of families filed returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge states/counties with insufficient taxpayers and omit or flag these from top-share calculations; prior studies (Schmitz & Fishback) faced such constraints for several states in 1929.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of relief spending coefficients (possible feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider reverse causality or feedback between higher inequality and more relief spending when interpreting positive regression coefficients on per capita relief spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors explore IV strategies and political instruments to address endogeneity; report instrument strength and consider that weak instruments may leave estimates imprecise or biased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data cleaning and correction of source tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate and correct published source tabulations (e.g., corrections to Mendershausen’s Appendix B totals) before computing distributional measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors documented specific corrections to county/city totals and bin sums (Providence, Racine) — ensure row/column sums match and correct transcription/aggregation errors to avoid biased ginis or transition matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of robust and clustered standard errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Report standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and clustered at the state level for regression inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors use robust clustered SEs in housing-gini regressions and other specifications; this accounts for within-state correlation across city/county observations.
